name: The Spec Reverse-Engineer
oneLiner: Reconstructs a feature's spec — description, acceptance criteria, scope — from its test cases alone, grounded only in what the tests evidence.
lead: Recovers the written spec when tests exist but the specification was never finished or was lost. Reads the test cases, groups them by story, and reverse-engineers a feature description plus a list of acceptance criteria straight from what the steps and expected results actually assert — no invented requirements.
chore: Documenting a feature that has dozens of test cases but no spec is slow detective work: read every test, infer the behavior each one proves, group by topic, then write a description, acceptance criteria, and in/out-of-scope notes. It's manual, and two analysts produce two different write-ups.
instead: The agent loads the test cases, buckets them by parent story, and calls the LLM to emit a description, an acceptance-criteria list, and in-scope/out-of-scope notes per group — constrained to what the tests evidence, never inventing requirements. Outputs Word, Markdown, and JSON.
whyItMatters: A feature with no spec is one nobody can safely change. Reconstructing the description turns undocumented behavior back into something the team can reason about and regression-test against.

howItWorks.step: Loads the test cases — from ADO (by feature, story IDs, or test-case IDs) or from an xlsx export.
howItWorks.explain: A precedence-ordered dispatcher: the first truthy source wins, so the checks double as a priority list. Offline `excelPath` is tried first because it needs no ADO connection, then the increasingly broad ADO paths — specific `tcIds`, then `storyIds`, then a whole `featureId`. The array checks are guarded with `&& input.tcIds.length` so an empty-but-present array falls through to the next option instead of resolving to zero test cases. If nothing matches it **throws** rather than returning `[]`, turning a misconfigured invocation into an immediate, obvious failure instead of a spec silently reverse-engineered from nothing.

howItWorks.step: Parses each test case's steps and expected results out of the stored XML.
howItWorks.explain: ADO stores test steps as an escaped XML blob, so this is a tolerant regex extractor rather than a real XML parse. `matchAll(/<step...>/gi)` walks each `<step>` element and, per step, pulls its `<action>` and `<expectedResult>` inner text; the `[\s\S]*?` (lazy, dot-all) is used instead of `.*?` precisely because step bodies contain newlines that `.` wouldn't cross. `stripHtml(...?.[1] || '')` removes the rich-text markup ADO injects, and the optional-chaining plus `|| ''` means a step missing an expected result degrades to an empty string instead of throwing. Crucially `idx` only increments inside `if (action)`, so numbering stays gap-free even when blank steps are skipped, and a step with no action is dropped entirely.

howItWorks.step: Buckets the test cases by parent story so each group maps to one coherent unit of behavior.
howItWorks.explain: Buckets tests into one spec section per parent story using a `Map` keyed by `String(tc.storyId)`. Stringifying the key is deliberate — it collapses a numeric `123` and a string `'123'` into the same bucket rather than two, and any test with no `storyId` funnels into a single `'ungrouped'` key so orphan IDs still get documented instead of dropped. `label` degrades gracefully: real `storyTitle`, else a synthesized `Story <id>`, else `'General'` for the orphan bucket. The `if (!map.has(key))` guard creates a bucket only on first encounter, so subsequent tests with the same key just `.push` — and `Array.from(map.values())` returns the groups in first-seen order, which keeps the output stable.

howItWorks.step: Reverse-engineers, per group, a description, acceptance criteria, and in/out-of-scope notes from the tests alone.
howItWorks.explain: Each group is reverse-engineered independently — one `callGeminiFlash` per story so the model reasons about a single coherent unit at a time. The prompt serializes every test's `[TC-id]`, priority, title and numbered `action → Expected` steps, then hard-constrains the model: return JSON **based ONLY on what the test cases evidence**, the guard against inventing requirements the tests never assert. The response is mined with `.match(/\{[\s\S]*\}/)[0]` — a greedy first-brace-to-last-brace slice that extracts the JSON object out of any prose or markdown fence before `JSON.parse` (note: unlike the other agents this uses raw `JSON.parse`, so a malformed response throws here). Finally the parsed `{ featureDescription, acceptanceCriteria, inScope, outOfScope }` is spread in **after** the trusted `groupTitle`/`groupId`/`tcCount`, and the real `testCaseTitles` are attached as provenance for every claim.

howItWorks.step: Serializes the reconstructed spec to JSON, Markdown, and — with `--word` — a Word document.
howItWorks.explain: Persistence with a filesystem-safe naming scheme. `label` is built by replacing every non-`[a-zA-Z0-9]` character in the feature title with `-` and slicing to 40 chars, so an arbitrary title can't produce an illegal or absurdly long filename; it falls back to `'tc-spec'` when there's no title. JSON (pretty-printed) and Markdown are always written under `input.outputDir || this.outputDir`, and the `${ts}` timestamp in each name makes every run a distinct snapshot rather than an overwrite. The docx is conditional on `input.word`, so `docxPath` stays `undefined` when it's skipped — and the returned object reflects that honestly, letting the caller report exactly which artifacts exist.

examples.caption: A password-reset feature with tests but no spec
examples.input: 18 test cases linked to a 'Reset password' story, covering valid links, expired links, and mismatched passwords.
examples.output: A description ('Lets a signed-out user reset a forgotten password via an emailed link'), acceptance criteria ('The user can request a reset link', 'The system rejects an expired link with a clear message'), and an out-of-scope note ('Two-factor re-enrolment is not covered by these tests').

examples.caption: A batch of loose test IDs
examples.input: A comma-separated `--tc-ids` list handed over with no other context.
examples.output: The tests resolved to their parent stories and grouped, each group rendered as its own mini-spec section in one Word document, ready for stakeholder review.

underHood.heading: Loads the test cases
underHood.input: A feature ID, story IDs, test-case IDs, or an xlsx export.
underHood.output: Test cases with title, priority, and steps — via the ADO REST API or parsed from the spreadsheet.

underHood.heading: Parses the stored steps
underHood.whenRuns: Per test case pulled from ADO.
underHood.input: The raw Steps XML on the test-case work item.
underHood.output: A numbered list of action / expected-result pairs, HTML stripped.

underHood.heading: Groups by story
underHood.whenRuns: Once, after all test cases are loaded.
underHood.output: One group per parent story — or an `ungrouped`/`General` bucket for loose IDs with no parent.

underHood.heading: Reverse-engineers the spec via the LLM
underHood.input: The group's test-case titles, priorities, and steps.
underHood.output: A description, acceptance criteria, and in/out-of-scope notes via Gemini Flash — constrained to what the tests evidence.

underHood.heading: Writes the specification
underHood.input: The generated specs, one per group.
underHood.output: Markdown and JSON always; a Word document too with `--word`.

prerequisites: Node ≥ 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
Read access to Azure DevOps and a **personal access token** (`ADO_PAT`) — OR an xlsx export of test cases if you'd rather not connect live.
A Google Gemini API key — this agent always calls the LLM to write the description and criteria.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program executed under Node. One-time install per machine.
steps.firstRun: First time on a new machine only.

steps.label: Clone the code and install dependencies.
steps.why: `npm install` resolves the agent's dependencies — the ADO REST client, the xlsx reader, the docx writer, and the Gemini client — into `node_modules`.
steps.rerun: No-op unless the dependency set changed.

steps.label: Set the environment variables.
steps.cmd:
export ADO_ORGANIZATION=my-org
export ADO_PROJECT="My Project"
export ADO_PAT=your-access-token
export GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-gemini-key
steps.why: Read at startup: the ADO org/project to query, the PAT that authorizes it, and the Gemini key that writes the spec. Skip the ADO vars entirely if you're loading from an xlsx file.

steps.label: Dry-run first — inspect the loaded test cases without an LLM call.
steps.why: `--dry-run` loads and groups the test cases as normal but skips the LLM step, so you can confirm it resolved the right tests before spending model calls.
steps.firstRun: Prints the grouping only — no description or criteria yet.

steps.label: Run for real, from whichever source you have.
steps.cmd:
# From a feature's test cases in ADO:
npx ts-node agents/tc-spec-agent.ts --feature-id 5001 --word

# Or from an xlsx export of test cases:
npx ts-node agents/tc-spec-agent.ts --excel ./inputs/test-cases.xlsx --word
steps.why: Drop `--dry-run` to call the LLM. `--feature-id` pulls every test case under a feature; `--excel` reads them from a spreadsheet — pick whichever matches where your tests live. `--word` also emits a docx.
steps.firstRun: Groups the tests by story, reverse-engineers each group's spec via the LLM, and writes the outputs.
steps.rerun: No change-tracking — every run recomputes fresh; re-run whenever the test cases change.

steps.label: Open the reconstructed specification.
steps.why: Outputs land as JSON, Markdown, and — with `--word` — a docx, one section per group of test cases.

inputs.name: --feature-id <id> | --story-ids <ids> | --tc-ids <ids> | --excel <path>
inputs.desc: The test-case source — pick exactly one.

inputs.name: --word / --dry-run
inputs.desc: --word also emits a Word document; --dry-run skips the LLM call and just prints the grouping.

outputs.name: TcSpec_<label>_<timestamp>.json / .md
outputs.desc: One section per group of test cases — description, acceptance criteria, in-scope/out-of-scope notes.

outputs.name: TcSpec_<label>_<timestamp>.docx
outputs.desc: The same content as a shareable Word document (only with --word).

runbook.rerun: No fingerprinting or change-tracking — every run reads the current test cases fresh and re-queries the LLM. Re-run whenever the underlying test cases change or after adding new ones; treat each run's output as the latest snapshot, not a diff against the prior one.
runbook.integrate: Reach for this when a feature has tests but no spec — hand the output to the **Requirements Sharpener** or straight to stakeholders as the 'what this feature actually does' reference. Works as a one-off audit tool or scheduled to catch specs that went stale.

video.caption: A 3-4 minute screen recording: point the agent at a feature's test cases and watch a reconstructed spec come back.
script: Open a terminal; have the feature's test cases visible in another tab for comparison.
Say: 'This agent works backwards — it reads the tests and rebuilds the spec nobody wrote.'
Run `node -v` to confirm Node is installed; one line on what Node is.
Run `npm install` (or note it's done); explain it grabs the helper libraries.
Show the `export` lines including the AI key; say this is the only client-specific part.
Run the command with `--dry-run`; show the test cases grouped by story, no AI content yet.
Re-run without `--dry-run`, adding `--word`; narrate as each group gets sent to the AI.
Open the produced Markdown; read one group's description and a couple of acceptance criteria out loud.
Point at the 'Out of Scope' section — explain it's inferred from gaps in the tests, not guessed.
Close: 'No spec existed for this feature ten minutes ago — now there's a defensible one.'
